papers.title_in_file: Variational inference with a quantum computer
papers.what_it_is: A paper that uses quantum Born machines as variational distributions for approximate inference in classical Bayesian networks, with an adversarial KL objective and a kernelized Stein discrepancy objective, tested in simulation and on a five-qubit IBM processor.

existing.value: The authors state that they use quantum Born machines as variational distributions over discrete variables and adopt two realizations: one with an adversarial objective and one based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy.
quotes: we use quantum Born machines as variational distributions over discrete variables.
we adopt two specific realizations: one with an adversarial objective and one based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy.
existing.certainty_reason: Abstract, and Sections IV A and IV B, state the two methods.

existing.note: Appendix A limits the claim: it discusses only representational power, not learnability, and leaves the construction of such a posterior to future work.
existing.value: The authors claim in the abstract that their techniques enable efficient variational inference with distributions beyond those that are efficiently representable on a classical computer. Appendix A states that they are discussing only representational power and not learnability, and that the construction of an intractable posterior from the prior and likelihood is left for future work.
quotes: Our techniques enable efficient variational inference with distributions
beyond those that are efficiently representable on a classical computer.
We leave this construction for future work.
we are discussing only representational power and not learnability, which is a separate issue.

assertions.value: The authors define the Born machine as a normalized quantum state parameterized by theta that outputs n-bit strings with probabilities given by the squared magnitude of the overlap of each computational basis state with that state, and to allow amortization they let the observed variables x play the role of additional parameters.
quotes: The Born machine is a normalized quantum state
that outputs n-bit strings with probabilities
we let x play the role of additional parameters.

assertions.value: The authors state that Born machines can be effectively regarded as implicit models: an unbiased sample is easy to obtain by executing the circuit and measuring the computational basis, but estimating the probability of a sample with multiplicative error requires exponential resources.
quotes: Born machines can be effectively regarded as implicit models.
it requires exponential resources to estimate the probability of a sample with multiplicative error.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing other work, that instantaneous quantum polytime circuits are Born machines with polynomially many parameters that yield classically intractable distributions in the average case under widely accepted complexity theoretic assumptions.
quotes: instantaneous quantum polytime (IQP) circuits are Born machines with O(poly(n)) parameters that yield classically intractable distributions in the average case under widely accepted complexity theoretic assumptions [81]

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Born machines have expressive power larger than that of classical models, including neural networks and partially matrix product states, citing other work.
quotes: Thus, quantum Born machines have expressive power larger than that of classical models, including neural networks [85] and partially matrix product states [86].

assertions.value: The authors state that Roth, extending results of Cooper, showed that exact inference in Bayesian networks with discrete variables is sharpP-complete, and that Dagum and Luby showed that even approximate inference is NP-hard.

showed that even approximate inference is NP-hard.

assertions.value: The authors state that MCMC methods have nice theoretical guarantees but may converge slowly in practice, whereas VI is often faster in high dimensions but does not come with guarantees.
quotes: MCMC methods have nice theoretical guarantees, but they may converge slowly in practice [9].
In contrast, VI is often faster in high dimensions but does not come with guarantees.

assertions.value: The authors state that implicit models are challenging to train with standard methods because likelihoods are prohibited, and that valid objectives involve only statistical quantities, such as expectation values, that can be efficiently estimated from samples.
quotes: Implicit models are challenging to train with standard methods.
Valid objectives involve only statistical quantities (such as expectation values) that can be efficiently estimated from samples [90].

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike the approaches that use variational ideas for thermal states and quantum data, and unlike those that encode Bayesian networks in a quantum state for exact inference, their inference methods apply to classical graphical models and classical data and are approximate and efficient.
quotes: In contrast, our inference methods apply to classical graphical models and classical data.
In contrast, our inference methods are approximate, efficient, and apply also to graphical models that are not Bayesian networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the scope of the methods.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing operator variational inference, that it uses mathematical operators to design objectives for the approximate posterior, and that suitable operators are those for which the minima of the variational objective is attained at the true posterior and the objective can be estimated without computing the true posterior.
quotes: Operator variational inference (OPVI) [96] is a rather general method that uses mathematical operators to design objectives for the approximate posterior.
(i) the minima of the variational objective is attained at the true posterior, and (ii) it is possible to estimate the objective without computing the true posterior.

assertions.value: The authors state that the KL divergence is an f divergence and the Stein discrepancy is an integral probability metric, that these two families intersect nontrivially only at the total variation distance as shown in other work, and that for this reason they choose the total variation distance as the benchmark in the numerical results.
quotes: As shown in Ref. [97], these two families intersect nontrivially only at the total variation distance (TVD).
It is for this reason that we choose the TVD as our benchmark in later numerical results.

assertions.value: The authors state that, taking F to be a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with the norm of f at most one, the supremum in the Stein discrepancy can be calculated in closed form using a kernel, and that the resulting kernelized Stein discrepancy can be calculated from samples of the approximate posterior alone.

assertions.value: The authors state that for n unobserved Bernoulli variables one possible kernel is the generic Hamming kernel, and that the kernelized Stein discrepancy is a valid discrepancy measure if the internal kernel is positive definite, which is the case for the Hamming kernel.
